title: Coordinates and straight lines: x = a, y = b, and checking a point
sub: You wrote this week: “x = 3 … it’s parallel to the y axis and vice versa.” That’s right. This week: why, plus where lines cross the axes, midpoints, and checking whether a point is on a line. About 20 minutes on screen, then the written paper.
target: AQA gives marks for working. Write the coordinates you used, substitute numbers into the equation, and check your answer against the picture.

sections.sub: Last week: dividing fractions. From memory. Think “how many fit?”

blocks.why: How many quarters fit into 3? Each whole has 4 quarters, so 3 wholes have 12. 3 ÷ [[1/4]] = 3 × 4 = 12.

blocks.q: Without working it out: is 6 ÷ [[3/4]] bigger or smaller than 6?
blocks.why: [[3/4]] is less than 1, so more than one [[3/4]] fits into each whole. Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger. (It is 8.)

traps.msg: You multiplied without flipping. Keep [[4/5]], flip [[2/15]] to [[15/2]], then multiply.

sections.sub: The equation of a line is a rule that every point on it obeys.

blocks.html:
x = 3 means: every point on this line has an x-coordinate of 3. (3, 0), (3, 1), (3, 5), (3, −2)… They all sit straight above and below each other, so the line is vertical: parallel to the y-axis.

y = −2 means every point has a y-coordinate of −2: (0, −2), (4, −2), (−3, −2)… The line is horizontal: parallel to the x-axis.

The trap: x = 3 has an x in it, but it is not parallel to the x-axis. And the axes have equations too: the x-axis is y = 0, the y-axis is x = 0.

blocks.q: Which point lies on the line y = −2?
blocks.why: On y = −2 the y-coordinate (the second number) is −2. (5, −2) ✓. Remember: (x, y), along the corridor, then up the stairs.

blocks.q: A line passes through (4, 1), (4, 7) and (4, −3). What is its equation?
blocks.why: What do the points have in common? Their x-coordinate is always 4. So the rule is x = 4 (a vertical line).

blocks.q: The line y = 5 is…
blocks.why: Every point has y = 5: (0, 5), (1, 5), (9, 5)… all at the same height, so the line goes straight across: parallel to the x-axis.

blocks.q: Where do the lines x = −1 and y = 3 cross?
blocks.why: The crossing point is on both lines, so it has x = −1 and y = 3: (−1, 3). Write x first.

blocks.q: What is the equation of the y-axis?
blocks.why: Every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0: (0, 1), (0, −4)… so the y-axis is x = 0. (And the x-axis is y = 0.)

sections.h: 3. Real AQA questions: axes, midpoints and checking a point
sections.sub: Three GCSE Higher questions you can already do.

blocks.html:
Crossing the axes. A line crosses the y-axis where x = 0. It crosses the x-axis where y = 0. Put 0 in for the other letter and solve.

Midpoint (the point exactly halfway): add the two x-coordinates and halve; add the two y-coordinates and halve.

blocks.q:
The equation of a line is y = 3x – 6

Circle the coordinates of the y-intercept.
blocks.why: The y-intercept is on the y-axis, so x = 0. y = 3 × 0 – 6 = –6. The point is (0, –6). (–6, 0) has the numbers the wrong way round: that point is on the x-axis.

blocks.q:
The equation of a straight line is 3x + 2y = 24

Circle the point where the line crosses the x-axis.
blocks.why: On the x-axis, y = 0. So 3x + 0 = 24, x = 8. The point is (8, 0). Check: 3 × 8 + 2 × 0 = 24 ✓. (0, 12) is where it crosses the y-axis.
blocks.ms: (8, 0) B1 (worked answer: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive)

blocks.q:
P is (4, 9) and Q is (–2, 1)

Circle the midpoint of PQ.
blocks.why: x: (4 + –2) ÷ 2 = 2 ÷ 2 = 1. y: (9 + 1) ÷ 2 = 5. Midpoint (1, 5). Check: from 4 to 1 is 3 back, from 1 to –2 is 3 back ✓.
blocks.ms: (1, 5) B1 (worked answer: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive)

blocks.html: Is a point on the line? Put the point’s x into the equation. Work out the y the line has there. Then compare it with the point’s y: bigger means the point is above the line, smaller means below, equal means on it.

blocks.q:
Is the point (2, 9) above, below or on the line y = 2x + 3?

Step 1: when x = 2, what is y on the line?

traps.msg: 9 is the point’s y. Work out the line’s y: 2 × 2 + 3.

blocks.why: y = 2 × 2 + 3 = 7. The line is at height 7 when x = 2.

blocks.q: The line is at y = 7 when x = 2. The point is (2, 9). So the point is…
blocks.why: 9 is bigger than 7, so the point is higher than the line: above it. In the exam, AQA wants the working (2 × 2 + 3 = 7, and 9 > 7) as well as the tick.

blocks.q: Explain why the line x = 3 is parallel to the y-axis. Give examples of points in your answer.

points.t: says every point on the line has x-coordinate 3, with at least two example points such as (3, 0) and (3, 5)
so the points are straight above each other: the line is vertical, the same direction as the y-axis

mark.note: Your daily sentence already said what happens. This adds why: the rule every point obeys.

blocks.html: Print the written paper and do it by hand. Write the numbers you substitute, and sketch a quick pair of axes when it helps. Answers on the last page: mark it yourself, then tell Papa your score.

items: I wrote coordinates as (x, y): across first, then up.
I know x = a is vertical and y = b is horizontal.
To find where a line crosses an axis, I put the other letter equal to 0.
To check a point, I substituted its x and compared the y values, and wrote the working.
I checked at least one answer against a sketch.

blocks.q: “Why is x = 3 a vertical line, when it has an x in it?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for “every point on it has x-coordinate 3, like (3, 0) and (3, 5), so they are stacked straight up”. If she says “because it’s parallel to the y-axis”, that is what happens, not why: ask “what do all the points on it have in common?”

paper.title: Maths Week 5: coordinates and straight lines (written)
paper.intro: Skill: written method and checking. Show the numbers you substitute. When it helps, sketch a quick pair of axes and check your answer fits the picture.

blocks.q:
1. (a) Write down the coordinates of three points on the line x = −2
(b) Write down the equation of the line through (1, 4) and (6, 4).
2. Where do the lines y = −3 and x = 5 cross?

3. Is the point (–5, –6) above, below or on the line y = 3x + 7 ?
Tick one box.

☐ Above      ☐ Below      ☐ On the line

You must show your working.
Do not use a graphical method.

Here is a statement.

A transformation that maps P to Q is a reflection in the line x = –1

Make one criticism of the statement.

Work out the coordinates of D.

6. Ali says, “The line x = 4 is parallel to the x-axis, because it has an x in it.”
Is Ali right? Explain your answer.

selfcheck: Q1: my three points all have x = −2 (the first number).
Q3: I substituted x = −5 and wrote the line’s y value before ticking.
Q5: I found the step from A to B, then used it twice more.

Reflection: which question did a sketch help with?

marking.html:
• 1. (a) Any three points with x = −2, e.g. (−2, 0), (−2, 3), (−2, −1) (1). (b) y = 4 (1).
  • 2. (5, −3) (1). Not (−3, 5): x first.
  • 3. (AQA June 2018 3H Q8(b)) When x = −5, y = 3 × (−5) + 7 = −8 (M1). The point’s y is −6, and −6 is bigger than −8, so Above, with this working (A1). A tick with no working scores 0. (Worked marking: the official mark scheme for this paper is not in our archive.)
  • 4. (AQA Nov 2019 1H Q5(a)), official mark scheme, B1 for any one of: says the wrong line has been given, e.g. the line should be y = –1; or says that for the given reflection the image would be in the second quadrant (the other side of the y-axis); or says the given line is vertical (x = –1 is vertical); or gives the coordinates of an image point, e.g. (1, 1) would move to (–3, 1). No mark for: “it should be reflected in the y-axis”, “it is not a reflection in x = –1” with no reason, or a right statement together with a wrong one.
  • 5. (AQA June 2018 1H Q7), official mark scheme: M1 for a correct step, e.g. x-coordinate of D = 0 + 6 + 6 + 6 or y-coordinate of D = 2 + 3 + 3 + 3; A1 for C = (12, 8), or D = (18, …) or (…, 11); A1 for (18, 11). (11, 18) does not get the last mark.
  • 6. No, Ali is wrong (1): every point on x = 4 has x-coordinate 4, e.g. (4, 0) and (4, 6), so the points are straight above each other and the line is vertical, parallel to the y-axis (1).
